evidence_items.publisher: The AI Innovator (summarizing The Wall Street Journal)

receipt.public_excerpt: AT&T saves up to 90% of AI costs by using open models, and plans to eventually run 70% to 80% of its AI workloads on them

evidence_items.explanation: AT&T was shifting AI workloads to open models for cost savings and planned to raise their share sharply. This matches the claim.

receipt.public_excerpt: AT&T has begun shifting significant portions of its artificial intelligence workloads away from Anthropic’s proprietary models toward open-source and open-weight alternatives

evidence_items.explanation: Reports that the shift was specifically away from Anthropic and toward open models, which fits Marcus's point about Anthropic's revenue.

receipt.public_excerpt: A corporate fad of "tokenmaxxing” on artificial intelligence (AI) technology is hitting its limits as workplaces throwing AI at everything are seeing the costs rise

evidence_items.explanation: Shows the retreat from tokenmaxxing that the claim calls a 'collapse.' The same report describes firms routing work to cheaper models, including open-source Chinese ones.

evidence_items.publisher: AI Weekly (relaying The New York Times)

receipt.public_excerpt: his internal platform now routes 40% of employee AI requests to open-source models instead of Anthropic's Claude or OpenAI's GPT.

evidence_items.explanation: After the post, AT&T's open-model share kept rising. It also notes Claude still handles harder tasks. This is context only because it falls after the target period.

unresolved_gaps: AT&T's own July 2026 blog post and The Information's original report could not be read, so the AT&T details rest on secondary relays of WSJ and The Information.
Specific evidence of other named companies switching to open models for cost is thinner than for AT&T.
'Collapse' overstates the reporting. Some analysts (for example SemiAnalysis) describe a shift to token budgeting rather than a collapse in spending.
